Her wears glasses, a black t-short and grey suit" class="wp-image-125867" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-04-at-08.03.37.png 1040w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-04-at-08.03.37-600x677.png 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-04-at-08.03.37-300x339.png 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-04-at-08.03.37-768x867.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1040px) 100vw, 1040px" /><figcaption> Francisco Correa Cordero. Courtesy Lubov, New York</figcaption></figure>



<p>Francisco Correa Cordero, who founded New York’s Lubov gallery, has died. The 37-year-old’s death was described as peaceful. </p>



<p>The gallery, which Cordero opened in Chinatown in 2017, represented a small group of artists, but has staged shows with many more. A recent exhibition by My Barbarian, the group’s first since a Whitney Museum solo show, featured work that ‘celebrate(s) queer, leftist agency’, <a href="https://artreview.com/my-barbarian-cat-suit-review/">Louis Bury wrote in <em>ArtReview</em></a>. Painter Kane Huynh is due to have an exhibition at the gallery in the Autumn. </p>



<p>The gallery’s roster features Theodore Darst, Bryce Kroll, Marsha Pels, Connor Marie Stankard and Harry Tafoya. Previously artists including Jenna Westra, Victor Boullet and pairings of Andres Serrano and Benjamin Bertocci, Jon Rafman and Parker Ito, have shown at the space. </p>



<p>Born in Mexico, Cordero came to the US to study photography at the School of Visual Arts, taking jobs and organising shows at Yancey Richardson Gallery, Martos Gallery, Aperture, Humble Arts Foundation, the Richard Avedon Foundation and Exit Art. He was Independent Curators International’s Executive Coordinator from 2015 to 2022 and served on the board of KAJE, an experimental exhibition space located in Gowanus, Brooklyn.</p>

<p><strong>Though these works might resonate with certain experiences of Hong Kong’s recent past, they’re far from political commentary</strong></p>



<p>Ellen Pau’s career survey at SculptureCenter is not as political as the circumstances in Hong Kong under which her work emerged – during the 1980s and 90s, between the signing of the Sino-British Joint Declaration and the 1997 handover – might suggest. Take the modest but charming single-channel black-and-white video <em>Operation Theatre</em> (1995), which plays on a monitor mounted high on the wall in the first gallery, as though part of a surveillance system. Semitransparent hospital workers and patients pass through a hallway, their forms rendered ghostlike, evoking the bleary-eyed vision associated with fever or illness in this gently altered but otherwise quotidian fragment. Similarly, <em>She Moves</em> (1988) – the earliest work in the exhibition and a quintessential example of video installation in the golden age of the form – is a wall-size projection showing raindrops sliding down a window. The projection is flanked by sheer curtains; a radio on the gallery floor next to an empty chair blasts the cloying 1939 British ballad <em>We’ll Meet Again</em>. Here and now, the song’s promise of reunion becomes less a foreboding allegory for the authoritarian rule eventually imposed on Hong Kongers by the Chinese government and more of an ironic soundtrack to sentimental wallowing. Though these works present psychological states that might resonate with or stand adjacent to certain experiences of Hong Kong’s recent past – waiting, being watched and grieving – they are, just in themselves, far from political commentary. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_129-1230x923.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-125852" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_129-1230x923.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_129-600x450.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_129-300x225.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_129-768x576.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_129-1536x1152.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_129.jpg 2000w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption><em>Pledge: Bik Lai Chu 碧麗珠, 1993/2018</em>, installation view. Photo: Charles Benton. Courtesy the artist, SculptureCenter, New York and Kiang Malingue, Hong Kong, New York</figcaption></figure>



<p><em>Pledge: Bik Lai Chu</em> (1993/2018) – one of Pau’s best-known works – and <em>Pledge: I Can Only Tell It to Strangers</em> (1996/2018) both deploy video recordings of Pau hunched on the ground in her underwear, rhythmically striking her head against the underside of a dressing table. Curators and critics have pointed out that the word ‘pledge’ here refers to both a popular line of cleaning products and China’s promise to maintain Hong Kong’s pre-handover freedoms, but if indeed Pau is simultaneously hitting her head against patriarchy and broken political promises, the titles are doing a lot of heavy lifting. The same could be said for <em>The Great Movement: Red Stock</em> (1996/2018), a digital projection of a nearly lifeless hand blocking a passageway in SculptureCenter’s mazelike basement. The title refers to China making shares of state-funded companies available on the Hong Kong stock exchange and the territory’s dependence on the resulting capital influx, but the hand alone doesn’t convey what the exhibition guide describes as ‘a sense of foreboding’ related to the economic situation. It just hangs there.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_068-1230x923.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-125851" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_068-1230x923.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_068-600x450.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_068-300x225.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_068-768x576.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_068-1536x1152.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_068.jpg 2000w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption><em>Where Have All the Flowers Gone 冇花 冇假</em>, 2026, installation view. Photo: Charles Benton. Courtesy the artist and SculptureCenter, New York</figcaption></figure>



<p>One of the newest and least resolved works in the exhibition, <em>Where Have All the Flowers Gone</em> (2026), is unmistakably bland and unfortunately so, right when the artworld is starting to pay attention to Pau’s long-term dedication to experimental video as an artist and curator. Evoking vigils and protests, its centrepiece, an enlarged candlelike form, displays a three-dimensional video flame that flares when viewers approach. Nearby, two common dinner plates feature thinly decorative designs generated by spinning a representation of the bauhinia, an orchid that serves as Hong Kong’s primary symbol, appearing on currency, on the regional flag and at pro-democracy demonstrations. The works engender none of the fear, exhilaration or solidarity of vigils or protests. At best, they resemble souvenirs from these events.</p>



<p><strong><em>Ellen Pau: </em>She Moves<em> at SculptureCenter, New York, <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://www.sculpture-center.org/exhibitions/14802/ellen-pau-she-moves" target="_blank">28 May – 16 August</a></em></strong></p>

<p><strong>A recent exhibition suggests that our drive to develop new technologies indicates a spiritual need to manage ‘existential uncertainty’</strong></p>



<p>This dense, heady show by Seoul-based artist Im Youngzoo is anchored by an hour-long, seven-channel video installation. Dispersed throughout the first gallery (of two), including a triptych of screens looming overhead and on a tombstone-like vertical monitor, <em>The Late&nbsp;故</em>&nbsp;(2025–26) follows scattered acts – a figure in a white Ghillie suit romping around in the snow, a woman receiving acupuncture on the crown of her head, a self-driving car navigating country roads, people visiting the cemetery – that sum up to what could be called, per one set of intertitles, a ‘survival report’, ‘a final witness’. While the seemingly disconnected scenes progress, typed texts scroll by. They include emails, weather updates, hypnosis prompts, stray thoughts about death and, in particular, questions about those who play dead.</p>



<p>A survival tactic shared by animals, as well as, the onscreen text points out, human organs (as in the case of hypometabolism) and machines (such as when a computer ‘halts its operation’ instead of opting for a ‘faulty execution’), playing dead is something visitors to Im’s exhibition can test out for themselves. In the centre of the first gallery is a long, stony grey platform. On it lies what appears to be a foil-covered corpse in a VR headset (<em>The Late VR</em>, 2025–26). But the platform also offers a niche for the not-yet-dead: to watch Im’s single-channel video<em> One Hundred Meeting Point</em> (2025–26), you withdraw into this single-occupancy alcove and stretch out on your back. A monitor on the ceiling inside plays animations starring an acupuncture dummy and a Buddha statue, with spooky footage of someone with a flashlight approaching you on a dark road. Other videos installed in cubicles on either end of the platform – such as <em>Waiting M</em> (2021), which collages, among other curiosities, footage from Mars with meditations on Soviet scientist Alexander Chizhevsky’s theories linking solar cycles to financial crises and political revolutions – invite viewers to kneel like mourners.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/The-Late-2026-installation-view-Photo-Jason-Mandella-1230x923.png" alt="" class="wp-image-123849" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/The-Late-2026-installation-view-Photo-Jason-Mandella-1230x923.png 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/The-Late-2026-installation-view-Photo-Jason-Mandella-600x450.png 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/The-Late-2026-installation-view-Photo-Jason-Mandella-300x225.png 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/The-Late-2026-installation-view-Photo-Jason-Mandella-768x576.png 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/The-Late-2026-installation-view-Photo-Jason-Mandella-1536x1152.png 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/The-Late-2026-installation-view-Photo-Jason-Mandella.png 2000w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Im Youngzoo, <i>The Late 故</i>, 2026 (installation view, Space ZeroOne, New York). Photo: Jason Mandella</figcaption></figure>



<p>As a whole, the show suggests that the applied sciences – pseudo and otherwise – and humankind’s drive to develop new technologies – for image capture, remote sensing, creating virtual realities and so on – arise out of a spiritual need to manage what the exhibition handout calls ‘existential uncertainty’. For nations, this angst might manifest as a technological arms race, and Im hints at ways in which governments, like South Korea’s starting in the latter half of the twentieth century, fuelled various tech frenzies, with mixed results. In the second gallery, whose walls are bathed in antiseptic yellow-green light, copies of a 1,254-page artist book, also titled <em>The Late&nbsp;故</em>&nbsp;– are displayed on a wooden platform. Here, Im writes, for instance, that when Korean president Lee Myung-bak proposed his ‘747 Plan’ during his 2007 campaign – a plan to increase the country’s GDP and per capita income, and transform it into the seventh largest economy in the world – ‘VR was tapped as a core technology in the strategy’. ‘The Ministry of Science and Technology announced an investment of one trillion won to “take the first place in the global VR market by 2015,”’ Im writes. ‘But with the Lehman Brothers’ bankruptcy in September 2008, the global financial crisis annulled all such ambitions.’ In view of this, <em>The Late VR</em> increasingly resembles not a wake for a headset-addicted human but a requiem for technological progress itself.</p>



<p>Then again, our devices don’t really die, even when they’ve outlived their potential. Opposite the platform in the second gallery stands <em>A Dark Room</em> (2025–26), three broken vertical monitors, and a further functioning one, mounted side by side like panels of a folding screen. Those that are switched on display haunting images, like the skirt and feet of a floating woman. Others offer nothing, until one notices the words of caution – ‘Beware of ghosts’, ‘Beware of science’ – smudged in Korean on their mirror-smooth surfaces. Maybe, Im’s clues suggest, some technologies are simply playing dead – withdrawing from us, transforming from coveted tools into vessels for our fears and longings, objects we in turn revere and contemplate.</p>



<p><strong>Im Youngzoo: The Late 故 <em>is on view at Space ZeroOne, New York though 25 July</em></strong></p>

<p><strong>Does any true wilderness still exist on this earth?</strong></p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Untitled-12-copy-1230x922.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-123111" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Untitled-12-copy-1230x922.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Untitled-12-copy-600x450.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Untitled-12-copy-300x225.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Untitled-12-copy-768x576.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Untitled-12-copy-1536x1152.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Untitled-12-copy.jpg 1890w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /></figure>



<p>The central question of <em>The Savage Landscape</em> is whether any true ‘wilderness’ still exists on this earth. Wilderness in scare quotes because, Cal Flyn reflects, the term is defined by human absence, but is largely contingent on human action. As we approach a point at which every spot of land will be explored and mapped, those territories that remain truly wild – savage even – are few, their existence largely determined by the grace of humans. Even the deepest ocean bed is becoming subject to the cartographer, forever the precursor to the despoiler, Flyn points out.</p>



<p>This book documents the Scottish writer’s travels, from the Brazilian Amazon to the Sinai Desert, Antarctica to Iceland’s volcanoes; her sublime descriptions of some of the most remote places in the world are a joy in their own right, but Flyn undercuts the travelogue with difficult ethical dilemmas that give the book a powerful, tricksy, narrative. She asks us to consider, for example, the plight of the Batwa people, shut out from their own territory in Uganda by the government and global conservation charities, some of whose staff have been found to commit atrocities against them (in neighbouring DR Congo), in the name of protecting the bush pig, the jackal and, most famously thanks to Dian Fossey and the film <em>Gorillas in the Mist</em> (1988), the great apes who make the forests their home (Fossey too was known to assault and torture in her efforts to maintain the gorillas’ peace). Things get even more ethically murky when Flyn accompanies big-game hunters in Mozambique – queasy-making wealthy Westerners who pay thousands to shoot lions and the like – but whose bloodthirsty dollars provide the necessary funding to preserve fast swathes of forest and wider species. She interrogates her own bias too, noting that she often feels ‘hampered by my own scientific training, my habitual clutching at rational argument’, observing that some of the best-preserved terrains have been protected not by research and education but by the mythologies of their indigenous people. The <em>yulsa</em> spirits of the Nepalese Bon people have offered more light-touch protection to their mountainous territory than any number of NGOs or government military might.</p>



<p>It feels that any attempt to escape the Anthropocene’s curse is doomed to failure; though fear emerges as one possible antidote. Not of the hysterical kind, but a precolonial respect for the unknown, a fear of predators real and imagined. For Flyn, the irony not lost on the author, the age of human exploration and documentation has been our greatest triumph and the world’s great undoing.</p>



<p><strong>The Savage Landscape: How We Made the Wilderness <em>by Cal Flyn. <a href="https://harpercollins.co.uk/products/the-savage-landscape-how-we-made-the-wilderness-cal-flyn?variant=56326664683899" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">William Collins</a>, £20 (hardcover)</em></strong></p>

<p><strong>What if artistic innovation emerges from material itself, rather than being imposed on it?</strong></p>



<p>The components are simple: sod and a body. The grassy panels, laid carefully over a person underneath, begin to pulse. This is <a href="https://artreview.com/ar-april-2018-feature-ana-mendieta/">Ana Mendieta</a>’s <em>Grass Breathing </em>(1974), part of a group of performances, recorded on video, that demonstrate the late Cuban artist’s inventive approaches to her environment. <em>Grass Breathing</em> finds new company in this exhibition, which gathers contemporary, often Latinx or Indigenous American artists whose practices stretch Mendieta’s ideas into the twenty-first century, enlivening unpredictable natural materials in similarly unconventional ways. Their grouping, an opening wall text declares, ‘celebrates kinship through a shared aesthetic language rather than fostering an ethnographic gaze or a desire for cultural authenticity’. Some unifying ideas emerge, particularly around nature’s ephemerality and its formal dictates, but the divergent array of artworks on view eventually strays from the exhibition’s compelling concerns.</p>



<p>Diné artist <a href="https://artreview.com/raven-chacon-what-does-america-sound-like-right-now-geeta-dayal/">Raven Chacon</a>’s aural composition <em>Study for Vertical Earth </em>(2026) fills the foyer: a thunderous, bass-heavy score, the result of underground microphones recording subtle earthly movements. Multiple artworks made using rocks, stone and sand greet the viewer upon entry, in turn highlighting the sanitisation of most institutional spaces. <a href="https://artreview.com/edgar-calel-balabaj-jaguar-stone-sculpture-center-new-york-review/">Edgar Calel</a>’s room-size installation <em>Ch’ablin nu rayb’el Chua taj ab’ej </em>(Splashes of My Desire on Top of Stones, 2026) stages local sandstone and lava boulders among mountains of brown dirt, each rock adorned with ceremonial offerings: dried flowers, eucalyptus and the artist’s own oxidised blood. In the next gallery, Jackie Amézquita further deconstructs the visual language of the museum: <em>Cuerpos terrestres en fluidez </em>(Terrestrial Bodies of Fluidity, 2025–26) features the destroyed remains of two monolithic, columnal sculptures, now broken into small bricks that resemble crushed pedestals, as though the museum itself were an ancient ruin.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Hammer-2026-04-06_023-1230x692.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-125737" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Hammer-2026-04-06_023-1230x692.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Hammer-2026-04-06_023-600x338.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Hammer-2026-04-06_023-300x169.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Hammer-2026-04-06_023-768x432.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Hammer-2026-04-06_023-1536x864.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Hammer-2026-04-06_023.jpg 1600w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>(left) Carmen Argote, <em>an archetype of touch</em>, 2025, avocado, cochineal and lemon juice on paper, 457 x 244 cm; (right) Carmen Argote, <em>an archetype of stillness</em>, 2026, avocado, cochineal and lemon juice on paper, 488 x 244 cm. Courtesy the artist and Commonwealth Council, Los Angeles</figcaption></figure>



<p>Others deviate less from Western artistic forms but use volatile, restrictive materials – often naturally derived ones native to the Americas. Carmen Argote, in <em>an archetype of stillness </em>(2026) and <em>an archetype of touch </em>(2025), has drawn gestural floor-to-ceiling depictions of human bodies using avocado mashed into an oily pigment – a substance that gradually destroys the paper beneath. Indigenous Amazonian artist Nereyda López crafts strikingly emotive figurative sculptures from <em>chambira </em>palm tree branches; <em>Ta+fe/Sacharuna </em>(2019) transforms one tapered frond into an indignant, hoop-earringed figure, its convex shape curving to form a chin, jaw and forehead. In some cases, an artist’s unique materials are difficult to discern, but require subtle alterations to gallery display: Peruvian artist and cosmologist Santiago Yahuarcani applies colour extracted from local plants – similar in appearance to that of tempera or acrylic – to papery tree bark ‘canvases’ to make vivid narrative paintings that must be kept in low light to avoid damage (<em>Bufeos robando mujeres en la fiesta del yacuche </em>[Dolphins Abducting Women in the Festival of the Yacuche]<em>, </em>2022).</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Nereyda_09-1230x1442.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-125738" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Nereyda_09-1230x1442.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Nereyda_09-600x703.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Nereyda_09-300x352.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Nereyda_09-768x900.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Nereyda_09-1310x1536.jpg 1310w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Nereyda_09.jpg 1706w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Nereyda Lopez, <em>Ta+fe / Sacharuna</em>, 2019, vegetable fibers and wood, 95 x 40 x 40 cm. Courtesy collection of Michael Krichman and Carmen Cuenca</figcaption></figure>



<p>Nature and climate change are recurring subjects, but not all works coherently engage these concerns at a formal level, particularly in later galleries. In Patricia Dominguez-Claro’s <em>Plant Saga </em>installation (2026), dried roses scatter decoratively, and incomprehensibly, alongside watercolour drawings of women and military drones. Others employ clay in order to explore personal history and experience, but this material choice feels incidental: Naomi Gamarra’s wall-hanging sculpture <em>Mirando arriba </em>(Looking Up, 2025) is an arched, decorative ceramic comb adorned with dangling clay lice, an eerie, if heavy-handed, exploration of ancient Peruvian bodily rituals and contemporary femininity that also feels out of place here. These works often deploy ancient ceramic techniques, but their methods have little influence on the results: Raven Halfmoon’s adjacent <em>Soku Sahyodahney’ah </em>(Caddo – Sun Twins, 2023) collages contemporary cultural signifiers with those of her Caddo Nation ancestry: two longhaired, conjoined ceramic figures – the ‘Sun Twins’ of Caddo origin stories – drip with graffitilike red and yellow colouring, the artist’s ‘tag’ scrawled across the back of their shared torso.</p>



<p>What’s most exciting about this exhibition is the idea that artistic innovation emerges from material itself, rather than being imposed on it – and that many sculptors, painters and ceramicists have long considered this challenge as more than a means to an end. But the energy present when I entered – lively chatter punctuated by Chacon’s guttural music – was not palpable as I exited through its final rooms, which overflowed with artworks that diverged from the exhibition’s earlier focus on material into explorations of identity instead. At best, <em>Several Eternities </em>vocalises the radical ‘shared aesthetic language’ of a growing force in contemporary art, but too often its inclusions dissolve into illegible survey.</p>

<p>The second edition of the Bogota Biennial, which will take place across the Colombian capital in September 2027, will be led by the biennial’s director Juan Ricardo Rincón Gaviria and chief curators Magalí Arriola and José Esparza Chong Cuy. Additional support will come from curators María Paula Bastidas, Juliana Steiner and Elkin Rubiano. </p>



<p>A Mexico-based curator and writer, Magalí Arriola was previously director of Museo Tamayo, Mexico City, and curator of the Mexican Pavilion at the 2019 Venice Biennale.&nbsp;</p>



<p>José Esparza Chong Cuy is a curator and architect from Mexico. He is currently executive director and chief curator of Storefront for Art and Architecture, New York. This year, he served as curator of the Kosovo Pavilion at the Venice Biennale.&nbsp;</p>



<p>The 2027 Bogota Biennial will explore the ecosystem of the city, exploring relationships between natural and built environments, and between human and more-than-human life. Alongside the exhibition programming, the Biennial will award $300,000 across 51 grants to local artists, independent cultural practices and institutions.&nbsp;</p>
</content:encoded></item><item><title><![CDATA[The Blockchain Fantasy is Dying]]></title><description><![CDATA[SoundCloud’s recently announced acquisition of NFT music platform Nina Protocol sounds the death knell for the illusion of tech’s utopianism in the arts]]></description><link>https://artreview.com/the-blockchain-fantasy-is-dying-soundcloud-nina-protocol-opinion-robert-barry/</link><guid isPermaLink="false">https://artreview.com/the-blockchain-fantasy-is-dying-soundcloud-nina-protocol-opinion-robert-barry/</guid><pubDate>Fri, 31 Jul 2026 09:02:18 GMT</pubDate><content:encoded>
<p><strong>SoundCloud’s recently announced acquisition of NFT music platform Nina Protocol sounds the death knell for the illusion of tech’s utopianism in the arts, says <em>Robert Barry</em></strong></p>



<p>The NFT died today. Or yesterday maybe. I don’t know. It seems like only yesterday that an artist named ‘<a href="https://artreview.com/why-nft-art-obsessed-bodies-madonnas-beeple-collaboration/">Beeple</a>’ was breaking auctioneers’ records with the sale of an image file bearing no physical existence beyond an impossibly complex alphanumeric glyph stored on a virtual ledger distributed across an unknowable myriad of hardware servers from Svalbard to Singapore –&nbsp;an NFT. And yet what could be more foreign, more jarringly anachronistic than the doleful sight of Jimmy Fallon and Paris Hilton holding up overpriced images of cartoon monkeys <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5zi12wrh5So" target="_blank">on late-night television</a>? A once much-shared social media post by a user named ‘toddkramer1’ <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://knowyourmeme.com/sensitive/memes/all-my-apes-gone" target="_blank">lamenting</a> ‘I been hacked. all my apes gone’ now resembles some terracotta tablet engraved in Linear B (that was a joke about Ancient Greek, by the way; not the AI productivity <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://linearb.io/" target="_blank">company</a>).&nbsp;</p>



<p>We seem to be experiencing an especially high turnover of futures lately. In fact, the hype carousel of Next Big Things may well be approaching terminal velocity. Musicians of a mind to keep an eye on such things will recall, in that hazy postpandemic interregnum, a great deal of media noise anointing nonfungible tokens as The Answer. Here, we were told, was the much-longed-for solution to the collapse of the traditional music industry at the end of the last century. In December 2021, mere weeks before toddkramer1 mislaid his virtual primates, <em>Time</em> magazine <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://time.com/6124814/music-industry-nft/" target="_blank">touted</a> the NFT marketplace as a ‘new model’ with the potential to offer musicians ‘financial stability, creative freedom and community all in one go’. The article, which followed similar panegyrics in <em>Forbes</em>, <em>Rolling Stone</em> and the <em>BBC</em>, cited a handful of case studies in which individual artists made thousands of dollars in cryptocurrencies selling selected tracks or shares in future royalties to fans and investors. ‘Time will tell’, the author Andrew R. Chow hedged, ‘whether music NFTs are a mere byproduct of a bullish crypto market or a transformative force destined to upend the music industry.’&nbsp;</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-30-at-16.47.14-1230x871.png" alt="" class="wp-image-125679" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-30-at-16.47.14-1230x871.png 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-30-at-16.47.14-600x425.png 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-30-at-16.47.14-300x212.png 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-30-at-16.47.14-768x544.png 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-30-at-16.47.14-1536x1088.png 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-30-at-16.47.14.png 1539w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Courtesy @ninaprotocol/Meta</figcaption></figure>



<p>With the recently announced sale of NFT music platform Nina Protocol to SoundCloud, that conundrum may finally be resolved. Launched in New York, also in 2021, Nina Protocol promised to provide ‘infrastructure for the next 50 years of music’. It was variously touted as ‘a revolution in streaming’ (<em>Rolling Stone</em>) and an opportunity ‘to cut out the middle man of private profit-oriented companies’ (<em>Dazed</em>). Artists were able to upload their music for listeners either to stream for free or use a cryptocurrency called Solana to purchase digital ‘tokens’ promising ‘ownership’, alongside various sorts of perks and bonus materials. The founders tended to avoid any mention of the initialism ‘NFT’, but to all intents and purposes Nina Protocol was an NFT platform. It stored its transactions on the blockchain. It dealt tokens. Those tokens were in no way fungible (they could be sold and exchanged, but not substituted or subdivided).</p>



<p>It was never entirely clear <em>why</em> Nina Protocol – or any of the other various schemes promising to democratise the digital music marketplace around that time –&nbsp;had to use blockchain technology. On the site’s own FAQs, the decision is explained as an opportunity to ‘free [artist communities] from depending on the policies of private companies’. Nina Protocol tended to position itself as if it were something like a musician’s cooperative, altruistically sharing the wealth among its members, but it remained a privately owned company with funding from American venture capital firms and European crypto investment funds. The schtick is familiar from the original music industry disruptors, Napster, who were all proud pirates and thorns in the side of the major labels –&nbsp;until they took $85 million in private loans and had a later sale <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://www.sfgate.com/business/article/napster-runs-out-of-lives-judge-rules-against-2774278.php" target="_blank">blocked</a> by a US bankruptcy judge. Nina Protocol’s actual sale price to SoundCloud has not so far been disclosed, but none of the artists whose work populated the site will be seeing a penny of it. When pushed, the company’s founders <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://www.dazeddigital.com/music/article/63054/1/music-streaming-platform-of-the-future-nina-protocol" target="_blank">expressed</a> their desire to avoid what went down with the sale and migration of MySpace, <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2019/mar/18/myspace-loses-all-content-uploaded-before-2016" target="_blank">when millions of songs disappeared</a> from the web more or less overnight. Nina Protocol’s Arweave blockchain, they claimed, was ‘designed around permanent data storage’. At the time of writing, there is no way to access any songs via Nina Protocol; users are encouraged to migrate their artists’ catalogues to SoundCloud.&nbsp;</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-30-at-16.49.50.png" alt="" class="wp-image-125680" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-30-at-16.49.50.png 1229w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-30-at-16.49.50-600x965.png 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-30-at-16.49.50-300x482.png 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-30-at-16.49.50-768x1235.png 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Screenshot-2026-07-30-at-16.49.50-955x1536.png 955w" sizes="(max-width: 1229px) 100vw, 1229px" /><figcaption>Courtesy @ninaprotocol/Meta</figcaption></figure>



<p>Because, despite all the hype, Nina Protocol shuttered its service in July this year. Its fire sale to SoundCloud should sound the death knell for the fantasy of democratising music via blockchain. Nina Protocol always felt like an attempt to tag a music streaming service onto the end of the NFT hype cycle. But even in their heyday, <a href="https://time.com/6124814/music-industry-nft/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">some blockchain boosters doubted</a> that the tech would ever be a great fit for music. Now, with 95 percent of all NFTs <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2023/sep/22/nfts-worthless-price" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">apparently</a> worthless, that fervour has dissipated – less a bubble than a hot air balloon. But tokenisation is just one in an ongoing succession of flash-in-the-pan technologies dangled with the promise to ‘save’ music through one neat technological trick. For over a quarter-century now, music has been presented as a problem to be solved and software as the solution to whatever that problem might be.&nbsp;</p>



<p>Let’s take the UK as a case study. While consumers now <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://www.nme.com/news/music/music-sales-hit-20-year-high-but-beneath-the-surface-uk-artists-earn-far-below-average-salaries-3827139" target="_blank">spend</a> more on music annually than they did at the height of the CD era and the UK’s music industry contributes some <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://www.ukmusic.org/news/new-report-reveals-uk-music-industry-contributes-record-8-billion-to-uk-economy/" target="_blank">£8 billion</a> to the national economy, the connection between fan purchase and artist payment has been all but severed. The Musician’s Union reports nearly half of working musicians make less than £14,000 a year. By comparison, a fulltime employee on the UK living wage could expect a salary of nearly twice that, at £24,784. Add to that grassroots music venues in the UK and US closing in their droves – and it all paints a pretty stark picture. But I can think of no dire situation, historically, which was improved by the addition of baroque speculative financial instruments, whether that’s the broader art market’s erstwhile embrace of NFTs or disastrous blockchain-financed movie thrillers (one of which <em>Variety</em> <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://variety.com/2022/film/reviews/zero-contact-review-1235277003/" target="_blank">called</a> a ‘steaming pile of nada’). The tech bros got us into this mess, privatising and sacking our cultural media. Why on earth should we trust them to get us out of it?</p>



<p></p>
</content:encoded></item><item><title><![CDATA[Winsor & Newton and Paul Smith’s Foundation’s International Art Prize returns for 2026]]></title><description><![CDATA[The third edition sees three early-career artists commissioned to produce work that will be on show at Paul Smith shops in London, New York and Paris]]></description><link>https://artreview.com/winsor-newton-and-paul-smiths-foundations-international-art-prize-returns-for-2026/</link><guid isPermaLink="false">https://artreview.com/winsor-newton-and-paul-smiths-foundations-international-art-prize-returns-for-2026/</guid><pubDate>Thu, 30 Jul 2026 13:42:56 GMT</pubDate><content:encoded>
<p><strong>The third edition sees three early-career artists commissioned to produce work that will be on show at Paul Smith shops in London, New York and Paris</strong></p>



<p>The International Art Prize returns for its third edition, commissioning three early-career artists to produce new works that will be displayed in Paul Smith shops in London, New York and Paris. This year’s winners are Bliss Coulthard (London), Jackie Liu (New York) and Axel Jonsson (Paris). Presented by <a href="https://www.winsornewton.com/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Winsor &amp; Newton</a> and <a href="https://www.paulsmithsfoundation.org/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Paul Smith’s Foundation</a>, the 2026 programme combines commissioning and exhibition with mentoring, professional development and opportunities to build international networks. Each city’s exhibition is accompanied by a public conversation bringing together the winning artist, their judge and <em>ArtReview</em> – the award’s media partner – to discuss mentorship, visibility, opportunity and the practical work of sustaining an artistic practice.</p>



<p>The prize was established to provide artists with sustained practical and professional support rather than a single award. Each winner receives a £1,000 grant from Paul Smith’s Foundation and £1,000 of Winsor &amp; Newton materials to make a new work in response to the annual theme, alongside bespoke mentoring, introductions to figures within their local art ecosystems and access to an international alumni community. The judges contribute their time without charge, while the wider programme continues beyond the exhibitions through business-focused sessions and videos produced by Paul Smith’s Foundation, on subjects including budgeting, communications, networking, social media and SEO. The prize, which has to date supported 18 artists from around the world, combines exhibitions and public programming with practical guidance intended to support the longer-term development of each artist’s practice.</p>



<p>This structure reflects the thinking behind Paul Smith’s Foundation, which was established in 2020 to strengthen the business skills of people working across fashion, visual art and design. It also builds on Paul Smith’s longstanding support for artists through scholarships, commissions and exhibitions, including a 30-year relationship with the Royal Academy Schools and a collection of more than 10,000 works shown across Paul Smith spaces.</p>



<p>This year, the artists were invited to respond to the theme <em>Making an Impression</em>, considering the experiences, encounters and influences that shape their work.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/4D7A9955-2-2-1230x1620.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-125598" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/4D7A9955-2-2-1230x1620.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/4D7A9955-2-2-600x790.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/4D7A9955-2-2-300x395.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/4D7A9955-2-2-768x1011.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/4D7A9955-2-2-1166x1536.jpg 1166w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/4D7A9955-2-2.jpg 1555w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Bliss Coulthard installation view at Paul Smith, London, 2026</figcaption></figure>



<p>Bliss Coulthard works primarily in watercolour, drawing on memories of love, loss and relationships to explore femininity and personal experience. The fluidity and unpredictability of the medium allow her to build dense, layered surfaces or dilute the paint into something looser and more atmospheric. Her influences include horror films, children’s cinema and the work of women artists.</p>



<p>‘There is a compelling intimacy and richness of colour to Bliss’s work that transports you entirely into another world,’ says London judge Katy Wickremesinghe. ‘Her preoccupation with femininity, memory and psychology manifests in a form of storytelling that feels at once naive and dark – deeply personal yet strikingly original.’ Wickremesinghe, founder of The Wick &amp; KTW and a trustee of the Royal Academy of Arts, Yorkshire Sculpture Park and Dulwich Picture Gallery, selected Coulthard for the combination of technical skill and originality in her work, as well as its potential to reach new audiences.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Brunch-of-Good-Fortune-1-1230x1848.jpeg" alt="" class="wp-image-125599" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Brunch-of-Good-Fortune-1-1230x1848.jpeg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Brunch-of-Good-Fortune-1-600x902.jpeg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Brunch-of-Good-Fortune-1-300x451.jpeg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Brunch-of-Good-Fortune-1-768x1154.jpeg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Brunch-of-Good-Fortune-1-1022x1536.jpeg 1022w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Brunch-of-Good-Fortune-1.jpeg 1331w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Jackie Liu, <em>Brunch of Good Fortune</em>, 2026, oil and acrylic on wood panel, 91 x 61 cm</figcaption></figure>



<p>Jackie Liu is a disabled and autistic Chinese–American painter whose portraits depict chosen family and moments of everyday pleasure. Combining vivid acrylic underpainting with layered oil paint, Liu uses humour, tenderness and close observation to consider joy and human connection as forms of resistance.</p>



<p>‘Jackie Liu’s work offers a compelling and intimate exploration of joy as a form of resistance,’ says New York judge Sergio Pardo López, ‘translating personal and collective experiences into vibrant, emotionally resonant paintings that capture the complexity and tenderness of contemporary life.’ Pardo López, Director of the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs and a curator and cultural strategist specialising in public art and creative placemaking, described Liu’s practice as grounded in lived experience while remaining ‘open and expandable’. He also identified the Prize’s mentorship as an opportunity for her to develop her technique, scale and professional positioning.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/IMG_1697-1230x1640.jpeg" alt="" class="wp-image-125602" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/IMG_1697-1230x1640.jpeg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/IMG_1697-600x800.jpeg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/IMG_1697-300x400.jpeg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/IMG_1697-768x1024.jpeg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/IMG_1697-1152x1536.jpeg 1152w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/IMG_1697.jpeg 1500w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Axel Jonsson’s studio, 2026</figcaption></figure>



<p>Axel Jonsson makes figurative oil paintings informed by history, mythology, literature, political events and personal memory. His compositions begin as imagined scenes, which he develops through drawing before building the paintings in multiple layers. His references range from Renaissance art and Impressionism, and his work finds inspiration in the work of El Greco, Goya, Böcklin, Soutine and Francis Bacon. Jonsson was chosen by Hugo Vitrani, a curator at Palais de Tokyo whose recent projects include exhibitions by Ali Cherri, Mohamed Bourouissa and RAMMELLZEE.</p>



<p></p>

<p><strong>Brutalism, according to the author, was a ‘method’ in Korea, where architecture was a response to the necessities of healing and rebuilding after twentieth-century wars</strong></p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Untitled-1-1-copy-1230x922.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-124205" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Untitled-1-1-copy-1230x922.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Untitled-1-1-copy-600x450.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Untitled-1-1-copy-300x225.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Untitled-1-1-copy-768x576.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Untitled-1-1-copy-1536x1152.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Untitled-1-1-copy.jpg 1890w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /></figure>



<p>In his last book, <em>Brutalist Japan</em>, writer and photographer Paul Tulett chased down Nu-Bru structures (that last ‘a term I’ve coined to partner with my more wanky <em>béton nécessaire</em>’) across Nippon. Here he elevates his passion to a fetish, rampaging across South Korea with his camera in an unselfconscious display of architectural onanism.&nbsp;</p>



<p>The original ‘Brutalism’ was originally coined in Britain during the 1950s to describe a new architecture that showcased monochromatic raw materials (particularly concrete), raw structures and stripped-down utility over colours, attractiveness and other ‘superfluous’ decorative elements. That stuff was all in the past and the past, with its dangerous nostalgia, so recently exploited by fascist regimes in Europe and East Asia, was out. Brutalism was architecture stripped bare: naked, honest, unpretentious and now.&nbsp;</p>



<p>If Brutalism was ‘a manifesto’ in the West, according to Tulett, it was ‘method’ in Korea, where architecture was all about a quick response to the necessities of healing wounds and rebuilding after twentieth-century wars (although, to be fair, this was also the case in Europe, but let’s not let that ruin the fun). ‘Concrete was the language of rebuilding’, he pronounces, getting back on track, and the overall aesthetic of the 100 structures he has photographed (some of them old, some of them ‘nu’) is, by and large, grey, often waterstained and full of cantilevers, pilotis, sharp angles and edges. Colour, when it comes, in the form of graffiti or the rings on Seoul’s Olympic Stadium feels rude and indecent.&nbsp;</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Sungnyemun_Gate_Seoul_1394_2_27260056438.jpg" alt="Sungnyemun. Photo: Richard Mortel / CC BY 2.0" class="wp-image-124204" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Sungnyemun_Gate_Seoul_1394_2_27260056438.jpg 960w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Sungnyemun_Gate_Seoul_1394_2_27260056438-600x399.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Sungnyemun_Gate_Seoul_1394_2_27260056438-300x200.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Sungnyemun_Gate_Seoul_1394_2_27260056438-768x511.jpg 768w" sizes="(max-width: 960px) 100vw, 960px" /><figcaption>Sungnyemun. Photo: Richard Mortel / CC BY 2.0</figcaption></figure>



<p>Bizarrely, Tulett starts with the decidedly non-brutalist curvy aluminium-tiled arcs of Zaha Hadid’s 2014 Dongdaemun Design Plaza (apparently there’s a ‘deeply Brutalist soul’ hiding underneath in the form of concrete stairwells and a ‘fortress-like substructure’). Later, he will go the other way and introduce the two-tiered-pagoda-style Sungnyemun (South Great Gate), constructed during the fourteenth century, reconstructed during the fifteenth century and restored in 2013 (at a cost of ₩25 billion, making it the most expensive restoration of a single building in South Korean history) as a form of protoBrutalism. One of the eight gates of Seoul is proof, for Tulett, that ‘Brutalism’s revival is no nostalgic gesture; it is a negotiation with identity’; that identity deriving from the ‘concrete heft’ of Sungnyemun’s granite foundations (the pagoda on top is made of wood) that forms the gate’s ‘DNA’. By the time he’s finished with it, indeed, Sungnyemun has become an expression of ‘cyberpunk’ aesthetics; which might be taking things too far. Indeed, what is and what is not Nu or even old Bru is not as black-and-white as it seems. Nevertheless, the bulk of the book comprises a more familiar parade of public toilets (Haeundae Beach), seawalls (Jeju Island) observation towers (Miradouro Sodae), art galleries (Arario), and plenty of private houses. And Tulett’s constant joking and punning: Japanese architect Tadao Ando’s Jeju Glass House is like ‘a meditative samurai’; the Asia Publishing Culture and Information Centre is ‘a building that feels edited’; the Eunpyeong Library is ‘where ideas bunker down’. Weirdly, while this can verge on the offensive, it gradually becomes mildly attractive (his photographs are beautiful): just another sign of Tulett’s puppy-like enthusiasm for the project. Even though, we learn in his introduction, that was the idea of his editor, rather than Tullet’s own: the whole thing having started when the former sent the latter a magazine article on concrete buildings in Korea. But aesthetics are more important than ideas in this book anyway. And if you can turn your pleasure into dollars, why not?&nbsp;</p>



<p><strong>Brutalist Korea: A Photographic Tour of Post-War Korean Architecture<em> by Paul Tulett. <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://prestelpublishing.penguinrandomhouse.de/book/Brutalist-Korea/Paul-Tulett/Prestel/e646027.rhd" target="_blank">Prestel</a>, £40 (hardcover)</em></strong></p>

<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Simone-Forti-1230x861.png" alt="" class="wp-image-125626" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Simone-Forti-1230x861.png 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Simone-Forti-600x420.png 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Simone-Forti-300x210.png 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Simone-Forti-768x538.png 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Simone-Forti.png 1350w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Courtesy Raffaella Cortese, Milan</figcaption></figure>



<p>Simone Forti, pioneer of postmodern dance, has died aged ninety-one, her gallery Raffaella Cortese has announced.  </p>



<p>Born into a Jewish family in Florence in 1935, Simone Forti had to emigrate with her family when Mussolini stripped Jewish Italians of their citizenship in 1938. Moving through Switzerland, France, New York City and Los Angeles, Forti then went to Reed College in Portland, Oregon, before dropping out and moving to San Francisco, where she studied with the dancer and choreographer Anna Halprin.</p>



<p>In 1959 Forti returned to New York City, where she met artists, dancers and composers of the downtown performance scene, including Robert Ellis Dunn, John Cage, Yvonne Rainer and Steve Paxton, and contributed to the early development of Fluxus. In 1960 she first presented her ‘Dance Constructions’ at Reuben Gallery then at Yoko Ono’s Chambers Street Loft Series. These ‘constructions’, ordinary actions prompted by cheap materials like plywood and rope, were influential in Rainer and Paxton’s founding of the Judson Dance Theater in 1962.</p>



<p>Following a one-year stint in Italy, where Forti spent time at the zoo and started integrating animal movements into her choreography, she returned to the US and taught at New York’s School of Visual Arts. Throughout the 1980s, she continued to develop her dance practice, pairing movement with language in what she called ‘Logomotion’ and creating performances in response to newspapers with her ‘News Animations’. In 1988 she moved to Vermont, where a community of artists had already settled, including her friend and collaborator Steve Paxton. </p>



<p>Forti returned to Los Angeles durimg the late 1990s, where she taught at UCLA. She gained institutional recognition later in her life, with her first major retrospective exhibition at Museum der Moderne, Salzburg in 2014 and the acquisition of her ‘Dance Constructions’ by MoMA, New York, the following year. In <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://artreview.com/simone-forti-receives-golden-lion/" target="_blank">2023</a> she was awarded the Venice Biennale’s Golden Lion for lifetime achievement. </p>

<p><strong>Sohrab Hura&#8217;s latest photobook captures conflict beyond the frame</strong></p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/SH_Snow_9-1230x1230.jpg" alt="Children playing in the snow" class="wp-image-120205" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/SH_Snow_9-1230x1230.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/SH_Snow_9-600x600.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/SH_Snow_9-300x300.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/SH_Snow_9-768x768.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/SH_Snow_9-1536x1536.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/SH_Snow_9.jpg 1575w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Sohrab Hura, from&nbsp;<em><a href="https://mackbooks.co.uk/products/snow-sohrab-hura?utm_source=ArtReview&amp;utm_medium=press&amp;utm_content=review&amp;utm_campaign=snow-sohrab-hura" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Snow</a></em>&nbsp;(MACK, 2026). Courtesy the artist and MACK</figcaption></figure>



<p>It begins in the harsh cold of winter: Kashmir, buried under thick snow; a man pulling two others on a sled; then a whiteout day during which the land is indistinguishable from the sky, the air dense with the wind-scattered ice crystals of snowflakes; a tiny silhouette of a lone figure just visible in the middle-ground; and in the distance, other figures – apparitions.</p>



<p>These are the opening images of <em>Snow</em>, which Indian artist Sohrab Hura photographed over five winters, until 2019, when the Indian government revoked Kashmir’s semiautonomous status bringing it under direct rule. That political rupture sits just beyond the frame. In a 2019 interview Hura noted, ‘I knew early on that my position was not to comment on the land’ as much as it was to comment on the fact that ‘I’m expected to claim Kashmir as my own’. Yet his images, which sit in the documentary style, suggest embedded, empathetic attention, attuned to how conflict settles into the rhythms of daily life.</p>



<p>Through the winters, people are pictured repairing sheds, commuting precariously atop buses, gathering hay. A woman pulls a woollen hat over a child’s ears; children play-fight with snowballs. There is joy in the candid photos of families, and guarded looks in the eyes of those who pose for portraits in the street. Hura is equally attentive to absences: plates of rice left uneaten; red plastic chairs abandoned in the snow; a half-written letter left by a window; accumulating interruptions, indicating lives paused or displaced, without explanation. As with his previous photobook <em>The Coast </em>(2019), Hura masters the art of sequencing as narrative. An image of a pile of terracotta bricks sits alongside one depicting a spill of crushed tomatoes; both echo recurring images of blood – on hands, in water, seeping into earth. The colour red moves through the whites of the book like a warning, surfacing and receding.</p>



<p>By the end, the suggestion of conflict sharpens: a line of women stand hand in hand, facing something, someone, outside the frame; a dark, viscous trail of liquid pools across the ground, its dark red tinge barely distinguishable from mud. Nothing is named, but the implication is difficult to ignore. Snow resists the clarity of reportage, offering something more disquieting: a landscape in which violence is ambient, absorbed into weather, into routine, into the act of looking.</p>

<p><strong>For <em>Pallavi Surana</em>, the Indian Pavilion at this year’s Venice Biennale raises both intended and unintended questions about what constitutes ‘home’</strong></p>



<p>National pavilions have long occupied an uneasy position within the Venice Biennale. Part exhibition, part diplomatic exercise, they offer nations an opportunity to project carefully constructed images of themselves onto a global cultural stage. The India Pavilion at this year’s Biennale embraces this representational function with unusual clarity. As Vivek Aggarwal, Secretary of Culture, and co-commissioner of the India Pavilion writes in the accompanying catalogue, the exhibition foregrounds artistic practices ‘rooted in India’s civilizational ethos’ through ‘traditional materials such as bamboo, thread, and earth’, carrying ‘the textures, memory, and quiet fragrance of the land itself’.&nbsp;</p>



<p>Titled <em>Geographies of Distance: remembering home</em>, the exhibition is jointly commissioned by the Ministry of Culture, Government of India, and private foundations associated with two of India’s most powerful industrial families – the Ambanis, who run the Nita Mukesh Ambani Cultural Centre (NMACC) in Mumbai, and the Munjals, who oversee the New Delhi-based Serendipity Arts Foundation, best known for the annual arts festival it organises in Goa. Uniting state patronage and corporate philanthropy, the pavilion arrives embedded within a broader project of cultural diplomacy, one that seeks to foreground continuity, heritage and national identity on an international stage.&nbsp;</p>



<p>Curated by Amin Jaffer, whose scholarship has long focused on the material and design histories of the subcontinent, the presentation gathers six newly commissioned works that meditate on ideas of home, memory, displacement and belonging. Throughout the exhibition, home appears not as a fixed geography but as a fragile condition capable of surviving the loss of physical structures. Jaffer has described this framework as autobiographical, reflecting his own diasporic relationship to India as ‘an inheritance of the spirit’ carried through beauty and material culture rather than physical presence.&nbsp;</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Alwar-Balasubramaniam-Not-Just-for-Us-2026.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù-1230x820.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-124081" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Alwar-Balasubramaniam-Not-Just-for-Us-2026.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù-1230x820.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Alwar-Balasubramaniam-Not-Just-for-Us-2026.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù-600x400.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Alwar-Balasubramaniam-Not-Just-for-Us-2026.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù-300x200.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Alwar-Balasubramaniam-Not-Just-for-Us-2026.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù-768x512.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Alwar-Balasubramaniam-Not-Just-for-Us-2026.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù-1536x1024.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Alwar-Balasubramaniam-Not-Just-for-Us-2026.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù-2048x1366.jpg 2048w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Alwar Balasubramaniam, <em>Not Just for Us</em>, 2026 (installation view, National Pavilion of India, 61st Venice Biennale, 2026). Photo: Andrea Avezzù</figcaption></figure>



<p>This logic becomes apparent upon entering the pavilion. A monumental semi-circular disk of cracked earth greets visitors in the first gallery. Titled <em>Not Just for Us</em> (2026), Alwar Balasubramaniam’s sculptural panel is formed from clay and soil sourced from rural Tamil Nadu. According to the accompanying wall text, its fissured surface records the passage of time and environmental forces, evoking ‘both the fragility and endurance of the earth beneath us’. Yet the cracks remain curiously unmoored from the conditions that produce them. Rather than pointing toward specific histories of environmental change, extraction, displacement, drought, or agrarian crisis, the fractured earth is presented as a universal metaphor for endurance.&nbsp;</p>



<p>Beyond Balasubramaniam’s earthwork unfolds a sequence of immersive installations. Ranjani Shettar’s bulbous floral sculptures are suspended from the ceiling, appearing, as per the wall text, as a ‘conceptual garden’ hovering overhead. Asim Waqif’s bamboo structure, <em>Chaal</em> (2026), a version of it first seen at the Kochi Biennale in 2022 and then at the Hayward Gallery in London in 2023, stretches upward into the architecture itself, and invites visitors to drum upon it, recline within it and physically inhabit it. Sumakshi Singh reconstructs her ancestral home through dense networks of suspended embroidered threads and lacework. Above, hidden on the mezzanine level, Skarma Sonam Tashi’s stacked papier-mâché houses recall vernacular architecture in Ladakh. A second monumental soil work by Balasubramaniam marks the exhibition’s exit.&nbsp;</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Ranjani-Shettar-Under-the-same-sky.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù-.jpg-1230x820.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-124082" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Ranjani-Shettar-Under-the-same-sky.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù-.jpg-1230x820.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Ranjani-Shettar-Under-the-same-sky.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù-.jpg-600x400.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Ranjani-Shettar-Under-the-same-sky.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù-.jpg-300x200.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Ranjani-Shettar-Under-the-same-sky.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù-.jpg-768x512.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Ranjani-Shettar-Under-the-same-sky.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù-.jpg-1536x1024.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Ranjani-Shettar-Under-the-same-sky.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù-.jpg-2048x1366.jpg 2048w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /></figure>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large is-resized"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Asim-Waqif-Chaal.-c-Joe-Habben-1230x820.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-124085" width="580" height="386" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Asim-Waqif-Chaal.-c-Joe-Habben-1230x820.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Asim-Waqif-Chaal.-c-Joe-Habben-600x400.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Asim-Waqif-Chaal.-c-Joe-Habben-300x200.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Asim-Waqif-Chaal.-c-Joe-Habben-768x512.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Asim-Waqif-Chaal.-c-Joe-Habben-1536x1024.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Asim-Waqif-Chaal.-c-Joe-Habben-2048x1365.jpg 2048w" sizes="(max-width: 580px) 100vw, 580px" /><figcaption>(top) Ranjani Shettar, <em>Under the same sky</em> (detail), 2026, handwoven cotton fabric, steel, lacquer. Photo: Andrea Avezzù<br>(above) Asim Waqif, <em>Chaal</em>, 2026 (installation view, National Pavilion of India, 61st Venice Biennale, 2026). Photo: Joe Habben</figcaption></figure>



<p>Each installation is dramatically spotlit and staged as a self-contained sensory environment within the pavilion’s darkened interior, with works suspended, elevated, or otherwise carefully choreographed to accentuate their apparent delicacy. Visitors weave between hanging forms, look up at precariously balanced structures, and move through spaces where shadows, textures and scale heighten an awareness of material vulnerability. The exhibition design repeatedly directs attention toward the physical properties of its materials – the brittleness of dried earth, the tensile fragility of thread, the flexibility of bamboo, the impermanence of paper – encouraging viewers to experience precarity as an embodied, sensory condition rather than as the consequence of specific political, social, or economic forces. The result is an exhibition in which instability becomes an aesthetic form: something to be encountered sensorially.&nbsp;</p>



<p>The limits of this formulation become apparent when placed against the realities of contemporary India, where the question of home is not merely emotional or metaphysical but intensely political. Attempting to define ‘home’ in India today is fraught precisely because the conditions of belonging remain deeply contested along lines of religion, caste and class. Across the country, domestic space is being violently remapped through religious majoritarianism, aggressive redevelopment, extractive infrastructure projects and accelerated industrial expansion. Muslim neighbourhoods are demolished as spectacles of punishment; informal settlements are erased in the name of modernisation; entire communities are displaced through corporateled development and ecological transformation. Against this backdrop, the question is not simply how ‘home’ survives loss, but who is permitted to remain, whose homes are protected and whose are rendered disposable.&nbsp;</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Skarma-Sonam-Tashi-Echoes-of-Home-2026.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù--1230x820.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-124083" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Skarma-Sonam-Tashi-Echoes-of-Home-2026.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù--1230x820.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Skarma-Sonam-Tashi-Echoes-of-Home-2026.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù--600x400.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Skarma-Sonam-Tashi-Echoes-of-Home-2026.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù--300x200.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Skarma-Sonam-Tashi-Echoes-of-Home-2026.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù--768x512.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Skarma-Sonam-Tashi-Echoes-of-Home-2026.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù--1536x1024.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Skarma-Sonam-Tashi-Echoes-of-Home-2026.-Pavilion-of-India-at-the-61st-International-Art-Exhibition-–-La-Biennale-di-Venezia-2026-©-Andrea-Avezzù--2048x1366.jpg 2048w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Skarma Sonam Tashi, <em>Echoes of Home</em> (detail), 2026, papier-mâché, clay, MDF board. Photo: Andrea Avezzù</figcaption></figure>



<p>Several of the works contain more specific social, ecological, and regional histories than the curatorial framing allows. Tashi’s suspended papier-mâché dwellings, for instance, draw on the architecture of Leh and the rapidly transforming landscapes of Ladakh, a region marked by militarisation, tourism-driven overdevelopment, environmental precarity and ongoing debates over political representation following the revocation of Jammu and Kashmir’s special constitutional status in 2019. The problem, then, lies not in the pavilion’s engagement with craft traditions or vernacular material vocabularies, but in the way vastly different material histories are flattened into a coherent and aestheticised image of India: ancient yet contemporary, spiritual yet modern, fragile yet enduring.&nbsp;</p>



<p>What makes this image feel particularly indigestible is the way the pavilion aestheticised precisely those material vocabularies most vulnerable to the conditions of contemporary Indian development. Earth, bamboo, embroidery, handmade paper, thread and craft labour appear throughout the exhibition as signs of continuity and civilisational depth. Yet many of the communities – rural, lower-caste, tribal, migrant and economically precarious – historically sustaining these artisanal traditions are also among those most exposed to displacement through infrastructural expansion, extractive industry, aggressive redevelopment and uneven modernisation.&nbsp;</p>



<p>India’s return to the Venice Biennale after a seven-year absence arrives at a moment when the country is increasingly invested in projecting itself as a global cultural and economic power, one defined not only by technological advancement and fiscal growth but also by a renewed emphasis on civilisational heritage. Within Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s vision of a ‘New India’, culture has become an increasingly important instrument of soft power, mobilised to communicate continuity, confidence and national pride on the international stage. Under the patronage of India’s most powerful corporate dynasties, the language of craft becomes detached from the social and material conditions that sustain it and repurposed as an instrument of cultural diplomacy. What emerges is an art-washed image of contemporary India: one in which vulnerability appears as material texture and the fractures of the present are absorbed into a reassuring narrative of national belonging.</p>

<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Takeda-花のような絵画_028-のコピー2-1-1230x1428.jpg" alt="Teppei Takeda, Painting of Painting, 2024. © The artist, Flowers" class="wp-image-102301" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Takeda-花のような絵画_028-のコピー2-1-1230x1428.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Takeda-花のような絵画_028-のコピー2-1-600x696.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Takeda-花のような絵画_028-のコピー2-1-300x348.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Takeda-花のような絵画_028-のコピー2-1-768x891.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Takeda-花のような絵画_028-のコピー2-1-1323x1536.jpg 1323w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Takeda-花のような絵画_028-のコピー2-1.jpg 1723w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Teppei Takeda, <i>Painting of Painting</i>, 2024. © The artist, <i>Flowers</i></figcaption></figure>



<p>The short review of this book would say that it does what it says on the cover, which is emblazoned with the words ‘Teppei Takeda Flowers’: it presents 34 paintings of flowers by Japanese artist Teppei Takeda. It’s a beautiful book (designed by Naoto Fukasawa), a little under .4-size. Each painting is full-page and features a single flower made up of a minimal series of brushstrokes that swirl partially mixed swathes of paint into a cluster of petals, the whole attached to a green stalk that looks like a supportive calligraphic gesture (if the paintings were sentences and the brushstrokes words, the stalks would be punctuation marks). The paint gives off the vibe of cake icing, causing a reaction not unlike the drooling triggered by one of American painter Wayne Thiebaud’s celebrated renderings of baked goods. Looking at the paintings, you can read the strokes and see the paint mixing, along with all other traces of their manufacture. Perhaps that’s why each work is titled <em>Painting of Painting</em>. But, of course, they look like particular flowers too. In a short text, Takeda states that the works are answers to the question of why he paints, which, in its circularity, appears to say something while actually saying nothing. For Takenori Miyamoto (all texts here are printed in English and Japanese), the paintings are a reflection of the artist’s personal life: being the primary carer for a young daughter. For Brian Dillon, they are a reminder of a Balzac short story and the disjuncture between abstraction and figuration (with segues to the work of Roy Lichtenstein and Jackson Pollock). But perhaps what this book really demonstrates is how much can be loaded into a single stroke of a brush. And in that sense it’s a reminder of why people fall in love with art.</p>
