<p><strong><em>Totems</em> comprises ten texts and lectures on twentieth-century European architecture</strong> <strong>written and delivered over the past 25 years&nbsp;</strong></p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_4914_mw-copy-1230x1640.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-123158" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_4914_mw-copy-1230x1640.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_4914_mw-copy-600x800.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_4914_mw-copy-300x400.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_4914_mw-copy-768x1024.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_4914_mw-copy-1152x1536.jpg 1152w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_4914_mw-copy-1536x2048.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_4914_mw-copy-scaled.jpg 1920w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /></figure>



<p>‘Modernists loved the slenderness of the airplane wing, but Neutelings Riedijk prefer [sic] the nonchalant swing of the elephant trunk,’ writes Irénée Scalbert in the title essay to this collection. He’s referring to a Dutch architecture practice’s unbuilt 1999 competition entry for the design of a concert hall in Bruges. This pithy, droll evocation is typical of the author’s approach in writings on architecture and, to a lesser but related extent, urbanism, painting and literature; it’s one of many flourishes here that encourage the reader to pause and consider a phrase’s merits and implications for the subject at hand, whether in a love letter to London’s least-loved airport (Norman Foster’s Stansted) or a provocative interrogation of similarities between a seminal postmodern design and a death camp (Aldo Rossi’s San Cataldo Cemetery and Auschwitz-Birkenau). In the case of the Bruges concert hall, the elephant becomes the conceptual basis for an argument that connects the proposed building’s profile, ornamented surface and ‘savage gravity’ to Napoleon’s fullscale plaster mockup for a monumental elephant on the site of the former Bastille. And that’s not to mention the many other threads presented along the way, including those of the lacemaking for which Bruges is known.</p>



<p>Presented in a format that comes close to matching the Michelin Green Guide my grandparents would have carried on visits to European museums and archaeological sites, <em>Totems</em> comprises ten texts and lectures written and delivered over the past 25 years that mostly address arguments, movements and figures in twentieth-century European architecture. More personally, one gathers, this is a guide to the main intellectual preoccupations of its author – a critic, historian and longtime lecturer in architecture programmes in London, Limerick and beyond. Quietly erudite, dry humoured, at times Socratic, at others mischievous, the texts argue opposing views, disguising the author’s views so that the reader, or student, may consider their own. There is a before-the-fall cast to this writing, which barely engages with today’s pressing ecological and political concerns, but it is a testament to the author’s thoughtful presence that I want to hear his views nonetheless.</p>



<p><strong>Totems: Selected Essays on Architecture <em>by Irénée Scalbert. <a href="https://www.park-books.com/en/product/totems/1726" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Park Books</a>, CHF 29 (softcover)</em></strong></p>
</content:encoded></item><item><title><![CDATA[‘Alphabet Book’ by Ali Kazim and Hammad Nasar, Reviewed]]></title><description><![CDATA[The book shows us that language is an evolving matter]]></description><link>https://artreview.com/alphabet-book-by-ali-kazim-and-hammad-nasar-reviewed/</link><guid isPermaLink="false">https://artreview.com/alphabet-book-by-ali-kazim-and-hammad-nasar-reviewed/</guid><pubDate>Tue, 28 Jul 2026 16:04:42 GMT</pubDate><content:encoded>
<p><strong>The book shows us that language is an evolving matter</strong></p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Untitled-2-1230x922.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-124216" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Untitled-2-1230x922.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Untitled-2-600x450.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Untitled-2-300x225.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Untitled-2-768x576.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Untitled-2-1536x1152.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Untitled-2.jpg 1890w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /></figure>



<p>Combining words and pictures, a <em>qaida</em> or alphabet book is a basic tool for learning language (Urdu in this case). In a <em>qaida</em>, objects become letters, letters become words, words and letters become objects: you slip between one and the other until language interbreeds with perception in the generation of thought. But as with all such tools, some are better than others.&nbsp;</p>



<p>This one begins with curator Hammad Nasar bemoaning the poverty of the selected words and images in the <em>qaida</em>s upon which he hoped to rely when it came to teaching his expatriate children Urdu (they learned to speak but not to read or write, apparently). Presumably it’s with that audience in mind that the Urdu in the <em>qaida</em> Nasar has produced with Lahore-based painter Ali Kazim is rendered in transliterated Roman as well as Urdu script. As much as that also reflects the more basic fact that English is the supreme language of art. Nasar’s introductory text is also in English, necessitating an awkward flip from the book’s front to its back for the right-to-left reading of the <em>qaida</em> proper. But games of form and function are partly what this book is all about. There’s no doubt that Kazim and Nasar plan to do the <em>qaida</em> better. Whether that be down to the choice of words, the construction of the images, or the choice of paper.&nbsp;</p>



<p>Featuring figures presented against flat monotone backgrounds, Kazim’s aesthetic, Nasar points out, combines influences from East Asian wash paintings, South Asian miniatures and European etching. We get to see how some of that works in the entry for ‘Khaaka – Sketch’, which shows four stages of the same work (a topless, middle-aged man holding a parrot) as it moves from outline to solid form, one layer at a time. In the process, the word ‘Sketch’ becomes richer: a study of change, contingency, evolution and incompleteness. The finished print appears in the entry for ‘Tota – Parrot’.&nbsp;</p>



<p>For Nasar, language is similarly evolving: he notes the Urdu words (among them pyjama, coolie and loot, included here) that have migrated into the English language, and English words that have travelled the other way. As well as the many other ‘linguistic rivers’ that flow into Urdu (such as Hindi, Arabic, Turkish and Persian). In parallel, Kazim’s illustrations reference the artist’s precedents and contemporaries, multiple faiths and histories. Where this book really succeeds, however, is in its suggestion that language is a similarly many sided thing.&nbsp;</p>



<p><strong>Alphabet Book <em>by Ali Kazim and Hammad Nasar. <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://ochrebooks.co.uk/book/alphabet-book" target="_blank">Ochre Books</a>, £39 (softcover)</em></strong></p>
</content:encoded></item><item><title><![CDATA[Betye Saar, artist confronting racist stereotypes, 1926–2026]]></title><description><![CDATA[The artist's assemblages confronted racist depictions of Black women]]></description><link>https://artreview.com/betye-saar-artist-confronting-racist-stereotypes-1926-2026/</link><guid isPermaLink="false">https://artreview.com/betye-saar-artist-confronting-racist-stereotypes-1926-2026/</guid><pubDate>Tue, 28 Jul 2026 15:49:00 GMT</pubDate><content:encoded>
<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Betye-Saar.png" alt="" class="wp-image-125544" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Betye-Saar.png 1200w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Betye-Saar-600x484.png 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Betye-Saar-300x242.png 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Betye-Saar-768x619.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1200px) 100vw, 1200px" /><figcaption>Photo: David Sprague. Courtesy the artist&#8217;s estate and Roberts Projects, Los Angeles</figcaption></figure>



<p>Betye Saar, whose assemblages confronted racist depictions of Black women, has died aged 99.</p>



<p>Born in Los Angeles in 1926, <a href="https://artreview.com/december-2016-review-betye-saar-black-white-blend/">Saar</a> first studied design at UCLA. After obtaining her BA, she worked as a social worker before returning to graduate studies where she discovered printmaking, the medium that dominates her early works. However, it’s for her assemblages that the artist became best known. Inspired by a 1967 exhibition of assemblage artist Joseph Cornell at the Pasadena Art Museum, Saar began collecting materials to create her own work: ‘I’m a recycler, or a hoarder, or a magpie’ she later said. ‘Certain things just catch my eye for whatever reason and I think, “I can make that into art.”’</p>



<p>Following Martin Luther King Jr’s assassination in 1968, her work took a more political turn. As a young mother of three, she couldn’t attend marches and used art as a form of protest instead. Her work was shown, along with that of other then-emerging and politically engaged Black artists like <a href="https://artreview.com/may-2016-feature-david-hammons/">David Hammons</a> and <a href="https://artreview.com/maren-hassinger-and-senga-nengudi-the-long-way-out/">Senga Nengudi</a>, at the short-lived Gallery 32 in Los Angeles. In 1972, she created <em>The Liberation of Aunt Jemima</em>. The assemblage reclaims a figurine of Aunt Jemima – the logo of an American food company rooted in racist stereotypes – by giving her a rifle and transforming her into a symbol of resistance. In 2007, the political activist Angela Davis said that the work had sparked the Black women’s movement.</p>



<p>From the seventies, Saar started gaining more widespread recognition for her work. First with a solo show at the Whitney in New York in 1975, from which followed exhibitions internationally. In the seventies and eighties, Saar also taught in universities in California, influencing a new generation of artists, including the painter <a href="https://artreview.com/how-kerry-james-marshall-restored-black-figures-to-the-western-canon/">Kerry James Marshall</a>. Throughout her seven-decade career, she continued to create assemblages and installations, intuitively incorporating objects and references acquired locally, through her travels, and from family memorabilia.&nbsp;</p>
</content:encoded></item><item><title><![CDATA[Oliver Beer’s Music for Paintings]]></title><description><![CDATA[The artist’s canvases record the shapes created by hundreds of notes like a musical score, but the closer you get, the less gestural they appear]]></description><link>https://artreview.com/oliver-beer-the-sky-in-the-cave-thaddaeus-ropac-london-review-robert-barry/</link><guid isPermaLink="false">https://artreview.com/oliver-beer-the-sky-in-the-cave-thaddaeus-ropac-london-review-robert-barry/</guid><pubDate>Tue, 28 Jul 2026 11:53:53 GMT</pubDate><content:encoded>
<p><strong>The artist’s canvases record the shapes created by hundreds of notes like a musical score, but the closer you get, the less gestural they appear</strong></p>



<p>The first time I encountered Oliver Beer’s work, he was standing facing the corner of the room in an old boiler factory on the outskirts of Paris, singing. His voice was soft, but at points the sound would swell, ringing out sonorously. He was pitching to the resonant frequencies of the space, the nodal points at which an acoustic vibration matches the natural rate of oscillation produced by the dimensions of an enclosed place, causing standing waves, as if the room were singing back to you.</p>



<p>That was at Thaddaeus Ropac’s Paris Pantin gallery in 2013. Beer’s work has been animated by the idea of resonance ever since. Recently, however, he has found more storied crevices to sing into. In 2024 he took a group of singers – including Rufus Wainwright, Mélissa Laveaux and Japanese soprano Michiko Takahashi – into the Font-de-Gaume cave in the Dordogne, the site of over 200 prehistoric paintings, in order to sing their earliest musical memories – mostly nursery rhymes and other traditional songs, recomposed and collaged by Beer into one continuous composition – to the elaborately painted and engraved walls. That journey became first a film, now a record, which plays from a turntable in the middle of the gallery in Ropac’s Mayfair premises, providing a near-constant soundtrack to canvases hung on the wall. As you view the paintings, you hear these plaintive voices, backed only by a deep, thick drone that sounds like an organ pedal, but that turns out to be just another voice, quietly murmuring the resonant frequency of the cave.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/DSF2440-Edit-1230x745.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-125518" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/DSF2440-Edit-1230x745.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/DSF2440-Edit-600x363.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/DSF2440-Edit-300x182.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/DSF2440-Edit-768x465.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/DSF2440-Edit-1536x930.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/DSF2440-Edit.jpg 2000w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption><em>The Sky in the Cave</em>, 2026 (installation view). Photo: Eva Herzog. Courtesy Thaddaeus Ropac, London </figcaption></figure>



<p>At first glance, Beer’s <em>Resonance Paintings</em> (all referenced here are from 2026) resemble the very wispiest of Romantic cloudbursts: we could be deep inside one of Turner’s storms or John Martin’s hellfire, zoomed in so close as to obliterate any surrounding context. Works like <em>Resonance Painting (Are You Even Real) </em>explode in crystal blues like a Raphael sky. <em>Resonance Painting (The Time Has Come Today)</em> blushes with a vivid, almost pornographic pink like the distended bodies of fallen sinners in a painting by Rubens.</p>



<p>The closer you get, the less gestural Beer’s works appear. <em>Resonance Painting (i saw you)</em> is shot through with serpentine striations that break up the soft-edged smear of the picture. In both <em>Resonance Painting (Pagan Poetry</em>) and <em>Resonance Painting (The Time Has Come Today)</em>, we see trembling horizontal and vertical lines meet and blur into fuzzy indistinction in a way that doesn’t look quite human, more like ripples on water or distortions on a liquid-crystal display. More than once I’m reminded of the weird curlicues that would turn up in early generative-AI artworks.</p>



<p>In fact, there is no artist’s hand here at all. Beer spreads dry pigment on his canvases then blasts them with musical tones. The structure of the vibrations causes the paint to spontaneously arrange itself into patterns, in the manner of Chladni, or sonorous, figures. Each canvas will record the shapes created by dozens, even hundreds of notes, and you can read the layers of consonance and dissonance between each sound in the distortions of the image. Less the records of painterly gesture, then; more something like a musical score, created using the same natural pigments (ochre, charcoal, manganese oxide) as the prehistoric Dordogne cave artists. The song, in a sense, remains the same. But even if you might baulk at such brazen appeals to timelessness, there’s an undeniable frisson to these works that flows from the acoustic vibrations that birthed them. Get close enough and all those strange squiggles will seem to dance in your peripheral vision. They are full of energy.</p>



<p><strong><em>Oliver Beer: </em>The Sky in the Cave<em> at Thaddaeus Ropac, London, <a href="https://ropac.net/online-exhibitions/246-oliver-beer-the-sky-in-the-cave/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">5 June – 31 July</a></em></strong></p>
</content:encoded></item><item><title><![CDATA[Guggenheim Abu Dhabi announces opening date]]></title><description><![CDATA[UAE cultural sector moves on in spite of war]]></description><link>https://artreview.com/guggenheim-abu-dhabi-announces-opening-date/</link><guid isPermaLink="false">https://artreview.com/guggenheim-abu-dhabi-announces-opening-date/</guid><pubDate>Tue, 28 Jul 2026 11:08:53 GMT</pubDate><content:encoded>

<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Kee-Hong-Low-Biennale-of-Sydney_credit-Daniel-Boud_079-1-scaled-1920x540-1.png" alt="Low Kee Hong" class="wp-image-125469" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Kee-Hong-Low-Biennale-of-Sydney_credit-Daniel-Boud_079-1-scaled-1920x540-1.png 960w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Kee-Hong-Low-Biennale-of-Sydney_credit-Daniel-Boud_079-1-scaled-1920x540-1-600x338.png 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Kee-Hong-Low-Biennale-of-Sydney_credit-Daniel-Boud_079-1-scaled-1920x540-1-300x169.png 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Kee-Hong-Low-Biennale-of-Sydney_credit-Daniel-Boud_079-1-scaled-1920x540-1-768x432.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 960px) 100vw, 960px" /><figcaption>Courtesy Biennale of Sydney</figcaption></figure>



<p>Low Kee Hong has been named as artistic director for the 26th Biennale of Sydney, which will open on 11 March 2028.</p>



<p>Low Kee Hong is <a href="https://artreview.com/manchester-international-festival-appoints-low-kee-hong-as-creative-director/">creative director</a> of the Manchester-based arts organisation Factory International. Prior to this, he was founding director and general manager of the Singapore Biennale, artistic director and general manager of the Singapore Arts Festival, associate artistic director of TheatreWorks in Singapore, and head of theatre, performing arts at the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority in Hong Kong. </p>



<p>‘My hope is to create an edition that feels generous, proposing new ways of assembly and rebuilding communities and celebrating our capacity for joy in these challenging times’, said Low Kee Hong in a statement. ‘The 2028&nbsp;Biennale&nbsp;will&nbsp;embrace participation and discovery,&nbsp;inviting&nbsp;people from all&nbsp;walks of life&nbsp;to share in the experience.’</p>

<p>Gunther von Hagens, whose ‘Body Worlds’ exhibitions of preserved and dissected human and animal bodies attracted some 58 million visitors over thirty years, has died. </p>



<p>The self-proclaimed ‘Dr Death’ developed his plastination method to preserve anatomical tissue in 1977 at the University of Heidelberg, a technique that removes the fluids from the body and replaces them with plastics that harden, but it wasn’t until 1995 that the first Body Worlds show opened in Tokyo. The exhibitions – which typically feature the preserved corpses in a variety of arrangements, as well as bodies cut through to show their internal organs – have since been staged in 168 cities. </p>



<p>‘I underestimated how long it would take for plastination to be a success. But more significantly I underestimated how big the success would be,’ von Hagens said. </p>



<p>The doctor’s shows have attracted considerable controversy and the attention of legislators worldwide. Von Hagens maintained that all the corpses were obtained ethically and legally, but previous reported incidents have included the bodies of executed Chinese prisoners finding their way to his laboratory in Guben, Germany, and in 2002 two Russian doctors were alleged to have supplied 56 corpses and more than 400 brain parts of dubious origin for plastination. At the time Van Hagens said he received the bodies in good faith and none were used in exhibits. </p>



<p>He also defended the ethics of showing the graphic material for a paying audience, emphasising an educational value: ‘When you can see beneath your skin you can see how fragile you are.’</p>



<p>The majority of the organic material was received from donors, with more than 19,000 consenting to their bodies being used. </p>



<p>It is understood the body of von Hagens will join them. </p>
